rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sign given to Moses is a divine proof that should remove Pharaoh and his courtiers’ doubt; sulṭān can mean proof, permission, or authority in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: was a divine proof given to Moses (sws) so that Pharaoh and his courtiers do not remain in any doubt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alongside Pharaoh, Haman and Qarun were prominent active opponents of Moses; both had been discussed in earlier sūrahs, and Qarun was an Israelite.
rows.anchor: two of his other prominent leaders ar e mentioned who were very active adversaries of Moses (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarun amassed wealth with Pharaoh’s government, and that wealth chiefly fueled his hostility to Moses; Islahi notes a strong similarity to Abu Lahab.
rows.anchor: there exists great similarity between his circumstances and those of Abū Lahab

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s opposition to Moses prefigures Quraysh’s opposition to Muhammad: as God routed Pharaoh’s chiefs, Quraysh will meet the same fate unless they desist.
rows.anchor: the leaders of the Quraysh are vehemently opposing him, in a similar manner, Moses (sws) was opposed by the Pharaoh and his chiefs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s party called Moses’ miracle sorcery and his claim to be God’s messenger absolutely false.
rows.anchor: regarded the miracle worked by Moses (sws) to be an act of sorcery and regarded his claim of being sent forth by God as His Messenger to be absolutely false

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh and his leaders should have accepted Moses’ true message and reformed, but instead ordered the killing of the sons of those who believed with him.
rows.anchor: the true message brought to them by Moses (sws) was to accept it and mend their ways

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They resumed the old policy of killing Israelite males and enslaving women because they feared Moses would organize the Israelites into a powerful nation.
rows.anchor: they gave orders to ruthlessly stick to the policy of killing their men and letting their women live in captivity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The policy began before Moses’ birth to keep Israelite numbers from threatening the Copts, yet it failed: Israel continued to grow until Moses openly challenged Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: This policy had been initiated long before the birth of Moses (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the scheme failed and Moses’ demand unsettled them, Pharaoh asked his courtiers to let him kill Moses and taunted Moses to call on his Lord for help.
rows.anchor: the Pharaoh sought permission from his courtiers to slay Moses (sws) and if he has a Lord who has sent him forth as His messenger, then he should call Him for help

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh claimed to fear Moses would change their religion or cause rebellion: monotheism challenged Pharaoh’s divine kingship, while Israelite organization could threaten the state.
rows.anchor: the Pharaoh was regarded by his people to be the manifestation of the sun God and his state was that of an incarnate king

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording let me shows Moses and his call had become so powerful that even a tyrant like Pharaoh could not seize him without his chiefs’ help.
rows.anchor: Moses (sws) and his call had acquired such might that it was not possible for even a tyrant and dictator like Pharaoh to seize him without the help of his chiefs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses entrusts himself to his own Lord and Pharaoh’s Lord against every arrogant unbeliever in the Hereafter; your Lord admonishes Pharaoh that God alone is Lord.
rows.anchor: he seeks refuge of his own Lord and that of the Pharaoh from the evil of every arrogant person who does not have faith in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arrogance is indifference to truth rooted in egotism and self-centeredness, themselves rooted in denying the Hereafter; such a person is a tyrant who crosses limits.
rows.anchor: Arrogance is actually the name of showing indifference to the truth which is the result of egotism and self-centeredness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer belonged to Pharaoh’s royal family, loved truth, and had sympathized with Moses’ reform before prophethood; after Moses killed a Copt, he warned Moses and urged his escape to Madyan.
rows.anchor: it was he who informed Moses (sws) about this intention and suggested to him to leave Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He embraced faith after Moses returned from Madyan but concealed it for a long time, apparently to serve Moses’ call more effectively from within Pharaoh’s House of Lords.
rows.anchor: for a considerable period of time, he hid his faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Had he declared faith earlier, Pharaoh could have publicly disgraced him as a national rebel and stripped him of his royal standing.
rows.anchor: the Pharaoh would have immediately made him a disgraced person before the whole nation by declaring him to be a national rebel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Concealing faith for religious benefit may be permissible, but becomes hypocrisy once religion faces decisive danger; the believer spoke openly when Moses’ life was threatened.
rows.anchor: when he saw that Moses’ (sws) life was facing danger, he gave up this cautious behaviour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s account addresses Muhammad’s contemporaries: once opponents plot to kill him, believers may no longer hide their faith but should openly support him at risk to life.
rows.anchor: now when their enemies are conniving with one another to kill Muḥammad (sws) it is not permissible for anyone to hide his faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer’s appeal that Moses said God was his Lord presents monotheism as an indisputable truth deserving support, not execution.
rows.anchor: to regard God as one’s Lord is an indisputable fact; if someone says so, he is expressing the radiant truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’ clear signs prove he is God-sent; only the blind can refuse to recognize his mission.
rows.anchor: The signs brought by Moses (sws) are a very clear proof of him being an envoy of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer reminds Pharaoh’s court that the Lord Moses represents is also their Lord; their error is treating others as lords beside Him.
rows.anchor: the Lord whose messenger he is declaring himself to be is also their messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Moses lies, the consequences fall on him; if he speaks truth, some threatened punishment will strike them, following God’s established treatment of rejecters and would-be killers of messengers.
rows.anchor: if he was lying in his claim to prophethood, then he will face its evil results and if he was true in this claim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional if he is lying reflects the audience’s supposed view, not genuine uncertainty; context and occasion determine whether a conditional conveys doubt.
rows.anchor: a doubt expressed in a conditional sentence is not always explicit in connoting doubt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not guide here means He will not let a liar and transgressor succeed; this apparently wise principle also sarcastically targets Pharaoh in front of his court.
rows.anchor: Here it is used to connote making a person succeed in his efforts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer tells the politically sovereign Egyptians that their power cannot save them if God’s punishment comes.
rows.anchor: Today you are politically sovereign in the land; you can do whatever you want to; no one can stop you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh interrupts, asserting that his proposal to kill Moses is considered judgment and the right policy, not an emotional or hasty reaction.
rows.anchor: he had done so after fully contemplating the consequences and that this was the right course of action

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the phrase lakum ẓāhirīn, ẓāhirīn is an accusative of state attached to the genitive pronoun in lakum, a construction found in earlier sūrahs.
rows.anchor: Many examples of such accusatives of state from genitive pronouns can be seen in the previous sūrahs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s interruption suggests he feared the believer would sway the court, so he tried to overawe it with his apparent sincerity, acumen, and foresight.
rows.anchor: he had assessed that if the speech of the true believer continues uninterrupted many courtiers would be influenced by it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ignoring Pharaoh’s interruption, the believer warns his people that harming Moses will bring punishment like that suffered by Noah’s people, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and later peoples who harmed their messengers.
rows.anchor: the same punishment will come upon you as came to the nations of Noah (sws), ‘ Ād, Thamūd and others after them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s refusal to wrong His servants means He mercifully sends messengers before punishment, giving people a chance to repent; rejecting and trying to kill the messenger leaves them responsible for their ruin.
rows.anchor: before sending any punishment, He has sent a messenger to inform them so that those who want to repent and mend their ways can do so

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh lived after ʿĀd and Thamūd, whose nearby histories were well known and could admonish his people.
rows.anchor: these nations thrived nearby. Their details were so well-known that they could be presented before people of the Pharaoh’s time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawm al-tanād means the Day of cries and shouts, aptly describing Judgment Day through the calls heard in catastrophe to flee or seize someone.
rows.anchor: I fear for you the Day of cries and shouts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fleeing language warns that those now plotting against God and His messenger will run from His coming punishment in vain; no one can rescue them.
rows.anchor: when God will attack them, they will turn and run away but this running away will be of no use

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer’s duty is to convey warning while acceptance is the audience’s choice; those God leaves astray cannot be guided, in accord with His established practice.
rows.anchor: his task is to only inform them of the good and evil; accepting this advice is up to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer recalls Joseph’s earlier clear proofs: the Egyptians doubted and disregarded his guidance because it opposed their desires, although reverence for their king kept them from attacking Joseph.
rows.anchor: they did not adopt a hostile attitude towards him; however, they did not value much the teachings and guidance they had been given

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They treated Joseph as a burden and felt relief at his death, thinking God would send no further messenger to restrain their desires.
rows.anchor: when he died they breathed a sigh of relief and became contented that God will not send any more messenger

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Pharaoh’s present misguidance follows his people’s earlier deviation: those who violate God’s limits, pursue desires, and choose doubt over knowledge are left wandering without guidance.
rows.anchor: the current state of deviation from the truth of the Pharaoh and his people are the result of this previous state of deviation from the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God further guides those who value intellect and moral discernment; those who use their intelligence to cast doubt on evident truths under desire have innate guidance withdrawn.
rows.anchor: Those who value these favours are further guided and led by the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Debate about God’s signs and directives must rely on proof; unsupported opposition is detestable to God and believers.
rows.anchor: Those who oppose them without any reasoning or proof are regarded as detestable by the Almighty and the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Needless hairsplitting follows God’s seal on hearts, making people lose direction and refuse clear truths that contradict their desires.
rows.anchor: those who indulge in needless hairsplitting do so because the Almighty has set a seal on their hearts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The seal stems from arrogance: conceited people resist guidance against their desires, reject prophets’ teaching, and imagine they deserve prophethood; people in Islahi’s time likewise mocked clear Islamic teachings.
rows.anchor: this seal is set on their hearts because of their arrogance and haughtiness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer challenges Pharaoh by prophetic admonition rather than boasting of followers, reminding him that worldly pleasures are fleeting and the Hereafter is the true home.
rows.anchor: in consonance with the way of the prophets of God, he reminded him of the Hereafter by telling him that the life of this world and its pleasures are but transient

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hereafterly punishment for evil is proportionate, with no excess; a believing man or woman who does good enters Paradise and receives abundant blessings.
rows.anchor: Those who reach there with the provision of vice will be punished commensurately so that no excess is committed against them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer addresses aristocratic leaders who likely served Pharaoh for temporary pleasures, urging them not to ruin eternal life for fleeting worldly gain.
rows.anchor: address of the true believer is to the leaders of the aristocracy most of whom must have wanted these transient pleasures of life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Context suggests Pharaoh interrupted the believer and other leaders objected that his message opposed ancestral idols and introduced a new religion; he answered with sympathy rather than engaging Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: the leaders of his nation also posed some objections on his speech

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He contrasts his invitation to salvation and the merciful, mighty Lord with their invitation to Hell and to associating partners with God without proof; God’s mercy and power are established, alleged partners require evidence.
rows.anchor: he is calling them towards salvation while they are calling him towards Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The true believer reasons that even polytheists acknowledge the one merciful God, but cannot establish His supposed associates without proof.
rows.anchor: even the polytheists believe in Him and there is no option but to accept Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression jaram lā means certainly or inevitably, and can also develop into an oath; lā negates benefit, meaning the invoked idols help neither here nor hereafter.
rows.anchor: This expression while evolving from this meaning also at times connotes an oath

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer concludes the idols are inventions: they grant no worldly or next-world benefit, all worldly gains come from God, and everyone returns to Him without those alleged deities’ protection.
rows.anchor: Beseeching or invoking them is of no use in this world or in the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who commit shirk wrong themselves and will have no intercessor but end in Hell.
rows.anchor: all such people will end up in Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer’s compassionate final warning says his people will later remember his advice, but too late; this refers both to the Hereafter and punishment for rejecting their messenger.
rows.anchor: you will definitely remember my advice in the coming phases, but at that time this will be of no avail

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By consigning his affair to God, the believer says he has finished his advice and leaves the audience free to respond, trusting God to protect and watch over His servants.
rows.anchor: whatever he wanted to say he has said and now his addressees can do what they like

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the believer’s speech, Pharaoh and his chiefs became enemies and schemed to restore him to their religion, but God protected him, showing that He safeguards servants who speak truth openly.
rows.anchor: the Almighty protects all His servants who declare the truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Āl Pharaoh means his family and followers; Pharaoh’s people faced decisive drowning, unlike earlier warning punishments during Moses’ mission that tested believers and disbelievers, and ḥāq indicates inescapable surrounding.
rows.anchor: This refers to the decisive punishment which caused the Pharaoh and all his armies to drown in the sea

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh’s people see Hell morning and evening in Barzakh before being ordered into its grievous punishment at Judgment; post-death conditions prefigure final reward or punishment, and grave punishment in Hadith belongs to Barzakh.
rows.anchor: in the life of Barzakh they are made to observe Hell every now and then so that they continue to keep in mind their real abode

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account also encourages believers hesitant to declare faith: in Hell, followers ask their former self-important leaders to share the Fire’s torment, but the leaders answer that all are condemned under God’s verdict.
rows.anchor: God has delivered a verdict between His servants
